attempts.label: DANDI:000404
attempts.entry_title: Invariant neural dynamics in a monkey cursor BMI (Athalye et al. 2023)
attempts.summary: Most of the main findings held in this data. Different population activity issuing the same command across conditions reproduced, as did invariant linear dynamics predicting that activity and the next command, each against shuffled controls. The simulations showing that dynamics reduce the input needed also held, except Monkey J's decoder-null result, which differed from the paper. The low-dimensional, decaying structure of the dynamics did not reproduce, as eigenvalue counts and Monkey G's frequencies fell outside the reported ranges. The nonlinear model comparison could not be run because its package would not install, and the files lack decoder matrices, so the decoders were recovered from the data.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Athalye, Khanna, Gowda, Orsborn, Costa and Carmena (2023) on dandiset 000404, which holds the binned spike counts, decoder state, cursor and trials of 9 sessions of Monkey G and 4 of Monkey J in a center-out and an obstacle-avoidance BMI task. It recovers the decoder from the files, compares activity issuing the same command across conditions with behavior-preserving shuffles, fits linear dynamics models that predict that activity and the next command, and simulates the optimal feedback control model of Figure 6 on the fitted dynamics. The rsLDS comparison was not run, as its package cannot be installed in a locked environment.

outcomes.notes: The rsLDS package the paper's code uses, ssm (github.com/lindermanlab/ssm at commit eb6c8aa33e5311d3564075807dec340759dd8081, or its only PyPI release, 0.0.1), cannot be installed in the entry's locked environment. Its setup.py imports numpy and Cython but declares no build dependencies, so `uv pip install`, which the registry uses to build the environment, fails with build isolation ('No module named Cython'). Outside the entry, with build isolation off, it installs. A timing run there, not part of the notebook, gave about 3 h of single-core compute for the criterion's design on the 4 Monkey J sessions (5 folds, K = 1 to 5, 10 Laplace-EM iterations). It gave about 35 h for Monkey G, most of it sessions 2 and 4 (110 to 115 units above 0.5 Hz). Monkey J alone would fit in two notebooks of about 20 minutes each on 4 cores if the package could be installed. Rechecked in the final revision with uv 0.13.6 at the code's commit, the build stops with 'No module named numpy'. The registry installs the lock file with a plain `uv pip install -r`, so the fix (no build isolation, or extra build dependencies in a uv configuration) is a change to the registry's tooling, not to the entry; the rsLDS comparison is left to a new attempt.

Every session's late mean is below its early mean except Monkey J session 1 (0.7656 against 0.7623).

outcomes.notes: Pooled LME slopes are positive with p < 0.001 for true distances (G slope 0.251, z = 38.69, N = 5509; J 0.129, z = 16.66, N = 1844) and predicted distances (z = 42.27 and 24.37); the paper gives z = 31.04 and 14.18 (true), 33.1 and 22.5 (predicted).

outcomes.notes: Pooled r is 0.774 (G) and 0.654 (J), slopes positive, p < 0.001; all 9 G sessions (session 7 at p = 0.046) and 4 of 4 J sessions are significant at p < 0.05.

The Full Dynamics Model needs less input than the No Dynamics Model in every session (ratio 0.44 to 0.91; Wilcoxon p < 0.05 in 9 of 9 and 4 of 4 sessions); LME z = -11.27 (p = 1.87e-29, N = 432) for G and -14.94 (p = 1.87e-50, N = 192) for J. Every simulated trial ends within 0.365 cm of its target. With Monkey J's velocity gain fixed to the summed 5 ms gain (sensitivity reading), the effect holds (LME z = -16.61, Wilcoxon p < 0.05 in 4 of 4 sessions).
deviations: Assumption for Monkey J. The paper builds Monkey J's 100 ms decoder from the PPF's parameters, not in the files; here its 100 ms cursor update is the least-squares update of the decoder state over each 100 ms bin (variance accounted for above 99%). Monkey G's is recovered exactly. The notebook also shows Monkey J with the velocity gain fixed to the summed 5 ms gain and the velocity rows of the cursor dynamics refitted.
The terminal weight 100 is the code's (behavior_co_obs.py); the dynamics are in-sample ridge fits on counts per bin.

outcomes.notes: Claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. The LME finds no difference (G z = -0.00, p = 0.998; J z = 0.02, p = 0.988) and no session's Wilcoxon test does (smallest p 0.069); the input ratios are 0.998 to 1.003. With Monkey J's velocity gain fixed to the summed 5 ms gain (sensitivity reading), the LME still finds no difference (p = 0.995) but Monkey J session 1's Wilcoxon test does (p = 0.0016), so under that reading the criterion, which fails on any session's Wilcoxon p < 0.05, would give not reproduced. The outcome therefore rests on the decoder reading for Monkey J; the fitted 100 ms update, which accounts for more of the 100 ms velocity (0.995 to 0.998 against 0.984 to 0.994), stays the adopted reading.
deviations: As fig6c-dynamics-reduce-input.

outcomes.notes: Under both nulls (1000 draws), the Full Dynamics Model's distances exceed the null (LME z = 25.4 to 26.0 for G, 15.5 to 15.7 for J; Mann-Whitney p < 0.05 in 9 of 9 and 4 of 4 sessions). Both No Dynamics models show no difference (LME p 0.83 to 0.999; no session significant). Decoder-null dynamics show none for Monkey G (p = 0.18) or in any session, but Monkey J's LME finds one (effect 0.016, z = 2.30 to 2.33, p = 0.020 to 0.021, mean normalized distance 1.09), so that absence is not reproduced. The LME here codes the simulation as 1 and the null as 0, so its z has the opposite sign to the paper's. With Monkey J's velocity gain fixed to the summed 5 ms gain, the result is the same: the decoder-null LME finds a difference (p = 0.0059 and 0.0051) and the other tests hold.
deviations: As fig6c-dynamics-reduce-input. Commands of the simulations are discretized with the simulations' own magnitude percentiles.

outcomes.notes: The criterion needs the point process filter's velocity update or its parameters and says the claim is blocked when the dataset has neither; the files hold neither (see findings). The notebook shows estimates in which the cursor dynamics are fitted jointly with the map, which favours the fit, so none is the criterion's test. Over all frames with the offset column in the fitted dynamics the map accounts for 98.92, 98.89, 99.57 and 99.25%; over the frames of rewarded trials 99.63, 99.63, 99.57 and 99.80% with the offset column and 99.10, 99.09, 99.09 and 99.63% without it; with the update taken as the change in velocity, 87.05 to 93.89%. The paper gives 99.6, 99.6, 99.5 and 99.8%.
deviations: Not tested. The estimated readings fit the cursor dynamics jointly with the map on the 5 ms decoder state, as the files hold no PPF parameters.

findings.statement: The files hold no decoder matrices (Kalman gain, steady-state cursor dynamics, the PPF's parameters), although the paper's Data availability lists decoder parameters among the deposited data. The code that wrote the files has these lines commented out (online_analysis/nwb_utils.py). Monkey G's steady-state gain and cursor update can be recovered exactly from the decoder state and spike counts (variance accounted for above 0.99999 on 99% of updates); Monkey J's PPF cannot, and its linear approximation must be refitted.

Monkey J's target_state and obs_details series carry one target and obstacle for every trial of a session; the writer indexes frames with the position of each go event in the event list (nwb_utils.py, targets[(go_ - start_index_overall):] with go_ an index into strobed), so the last trial's values fill the file. In Monkey G's sessions 0 and 1, checked, target_state at reward is one value for all trials and does not hold the trial's target. Targets have to be read from the cursor position at reward.

The trials table has only start and stop times. Task, target, direction around the obstacle and Monkey J's obstacle trial type are not given; the task can be read from the obstacle series of each task entry, the target from the cursor at reward, and Monkey J's obstacle trial types (the paper analyses only partial and full obstruction) only by matching start and end positions to a target list in the paper's code.

Units differ within Monkey J's files. The cursor and decoder state are in m and m/s, while target_state, obstacle_position and obs_details are stated in cm; target_state holds center-out targets in m (0.1027, 0.1384) and obstacle-task targets in cm (-3.25, 8.13) under that one unit. Monkey G's files are in cm throughout.

Question for the authors. How was Monkey J's 100 ms decoder for the simulations built (the expression for F in Methods, "BMI cursor dynamics", does not survive in the text), and in what units are the next-command errors of Table S1 (row 5E)? Here the 100 ms cursor update was fitted to the decoder state, and the errors match the paper's only when multiplied by 10.

Monkey G's decoder state does not follow the steady-state filter on 0.03 to 0.95% of updates per session, among them the first updates of each task entry, where the filter had not converged. The gain recovered on the other updates accounts for 0.928 to 1 of the variance of the velocity update over all updates, so the gain must be fitted on the updates the filter explains.
